# Introduction
Financial markets do not behave consistently over time, as periods of growth, decline, stability, and high volatility can occur under different market conditions.
To describe these market conditions more precisely, we define three market regimes: bull, bear and consolidation/sideways.
A bear market regime occurs when stock prices decline by 20% or more from a recent peak over a sustained period of time.
A bull market regime occurs when stock prices rise 20% or more from a recent low over a sustained period of time.
A sideways market regime occurs when stock prices fluctuate up and down within a narrow range.
An important distinction is that these market regimes are not directly observable. 
We can observe stock prices and returns, but we cannot directly observe whether the market is currently in a bull, bear, or sideways regime.

Due to the "hidden" nature of the stock market regimes, Hidden Markov Models provide a helpful framework for identifying and analysing these unobservable regimes.
Hidden Markov models can be used to identify the likelihood of moving between market regimes and the signals given by the market (stock-prices) that define each state.
The primary objective of this project is to use both simulated and real-world stock-market data to fit a Hidden Markov Model, and interpret the characteristics and transition probabilities of the regimes it identifies.

The rest of this project is as follows. Section 2 reviews the theory of Markov chains and Hidden Markov Models.
Section 3 presents the simulation study and real stock-market data application (all code and outputs will be in an Appendix).
Section 4 summarizes the main findings and limitations of the project, followed by References in section 5.
